title: Lior and the Uniform
premise: In the winter of 1916, Sable Ishikawa serves as a nurse at a riverfront hospital where she secretly records the names of wounded soldiers that officers leave out of official reports, believing she is keeping history honest from the margins. When Emil Voss, a wounded foreign national carrying a letter in the unmistakable handwriting of her presumed-dead brother Jun, arrives under guard, she learns Jun survived the war's early slaughter and is now interned as an enemy alien across the frozen river. To honor a childhood promise the siblings made in peacetime—that neither would ever be buried without the other knowing—Sable must smuggle Emil's message across the ice before the spring thaw makes the crossing impossible and the war's bureaucracy erases Jun forever. She succeeds at devastating cost, losing her post and her invisibility, but the novel ends with Jun's reply arriving as the ice breaks, and Sable choosing to keep her ledger, now as testimony rather than secret.
about_author: Elodie Fairweather is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime hospital records and became haunted by the names that appeared in no official document. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous,' and lives near a river that freezes every winter.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Introduces the riverfront hospital in winter 1916, her nightly ritual of recording omitted names, and her philosophy that history happens elsewhere, to other people. Emotional beat: quiet, controlled detachment that the reader will watch fracture.

chapters.title: Names the Officers Omit
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. A convoy of wounded arrives; she witnesses an officer strike three names from the intake list, including a dying boy. She adds them to her ledger. Emotional beat: the first flicker of anger beneath her practiced neutrality.

chapters.title: A Letter Written in Jun's Hand
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. A guard delivers a prisoner with a shrapnel wound—Emil Voss, an interned foreign national—who presses a folded letter into her hand. The handwriting is unmistakably her brother Jun's, declared dead two years ago. Emotional beat: the floor drops out of her ordered world.

chapters.title: What Emil Carried
chapters.summary: Emil's POV. Flashback to how Emil met Jun in an internment camp across the river, their fragile friendship, and Jun's plea that if Emil ever crossed, he find the nurse with the ledger. Emotional beat: grief and loyalty entangled.

chapters.title: The Promise Made in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, interwoven with memory. Childhood on the river with Jun: the pact that neither would be buried without the other knowing, sworn on a summer afternoon that now feels like another country. Emotional beat: tenderness sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Enemy Across the Ice
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She studies the frozen river from the hospital window, learning the guard rotations, the ice's color and sound. Officially, Jun is dead; officially, crossing is treason. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into method.

chapters.title: The Matron Suspects
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Head Matron Grell notices Sable's late rounds and the extra candle wax. A cat-and-mouse conversation in which Grell reveals she once lost a brother to a war that misspelled his name. Emotional beat: an ambiguous ally, not yet trusted.

chapters.title: Treating the Messenger
chapters.summary: Alternating Sable and Emil POV. Sable nurses Emil back toward discharge-and-transfer, which would end her access to him. They trade fragments of Jun—his laugh, his terrible singing, his insistence that Sable never learned to lose gracefully. Emotional beat: two strangers bound by a third man's hope.

chapters.title: The Officer Who Writes History
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Colonel Ashe, the man who strikes names from lists, arrives to inspect and announces Emil will be transferred in ten days. Sable realizes her clock is the ice, the transfer, and Ashe's attention all at once. Emotional beat: dread with a deadline.

chapters.title: Learning the River
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She bribes a lamplighter for the patrol schedule and walks the bank at night, mapping pressure ridges and thin black patches. Emotional beat: her invisibility, once a shield, becomes a tool.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Costs
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Ashe discovers discrepancies in the intake records and interrogates the staff. Sable watches an orderly take the blame for a name she recorded. Emotional beat: guilt—the first true price of her secret.

chapters.title: Emil's Bargain
chapters.summary: Emil's POV. Facing transfer to a harsher camp, Emil offers Sable the last piece of Jun: a map of the internment camp drawn from memory, and the confession that Jun is ill. Emotional beat: urgency hardening into desperation.

chapters.title: Grell's Choice
chapters.summary: Sable and Grell POV. Sable, out of options, half-confesses. Grell neither reports her nor agrees to help, but leaves the pharmacy unlocked and a vial of laudanum on the shelf. Emotional beat: solidarity expressed in silence.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Thaw
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The river groans; the ice is failing early. Ashe moves Emil's transfer up to dawn. Sable must cross tonight with the letter, the map, and Jun's promise. Emotional beat: terror and clarity arriving together.

chapters.title: Crossing
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, the novel's set-piece. The night crossing: cracking ice, a patrol lamp sweeping, a fall through a pressure ridge that soaks her to the waist, the far bank reached with the letter dry inside her coat. Emotional beat: pure survival, promise made flesh.

chapters.title: The Camp of the Forgotten
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She poses as a Red Cross relief worker to enter the internment camp and finds Jun alive but weakened, in the infirmary. The reunion is quiet, furious, and tender—he is angry she came. Emotional beat: love and duty colliding at last.

chapters.title: The Argument on the Far Bank
chapters.summary: Sable and Jun POV. Jun refuses to let her risk returning for him; Sable refuses to leave without a plan. They forge one: Grell's contact in the relief service, papers, the spring exchange lists. Emotional beat: sibling war and sibling peace in a single conversation.

chapters.title: Return at Dawn
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She recrosses the rotten ice as the thaw begins, nearly too late, and walks into Ashe waiting at the hospital door. Emotional beat: the trap she always knew existed, finally sprung.

chapters.title: Ashe's Offer
chapters.summary: Sable and Ashe POV. Ashe offers her a choice: surrender the ledger and Jun stays a dead man on paper—safe, erased—or she confesses, and both face tribunal. Sable realizes Ashe's erasures were never malice but cowardice. Emotional beat: the theme made explicit—memory versus duty.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Names
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, climax. Rather than surrender the ledger or confess alone, she reads the omitted names aloud in the ward at rounds, in front of Grell, the orderlies, and Ashe—each name a small insurrection she cannot be punished for without proving true. Emotional beat: the invisible made undeniable.

chapters.title: What the Ice Breaks Open
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Stripped of her post but not prosecuted—Grell's testimony and public sentiment protect her—Sable packs her things as the river finally breaks, great plates grinding downstream. A relief-service envelope arrives bearing Jun's handwriting: the exchange list includes his name. Emotional beat: grief and joy in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Ledger, Kept
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, resolution. On the station platform, Jun steps off the train thin and alive; Emil, released in a later exchange, finds them both a year later. Sable begins a new ledger—not of the omitted, but of the found—and writes the first name herself. Emotional beat: inheritance transformed; memory as a living act, not a secret.
